examples.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14043620/assets/62dec67282c5bc2707377cb976412a48ca3c41ffeed6aa74ef0d5b1ef8d6e380.png)

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} ,$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v) = 2v\cos{u}$ and $y(u,v) = v\sin{u}.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =-2v\operatorname{sin}⁡u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡u \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =v\operatorname{cos}⁡u & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡u\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-2v\operatorname{sin}⁡u & 2\operatorname{cos}⁡u \\ v\operatorname{cos}⁡u & \operatorname{sin}⁡u\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2v\operatorname{sin}⁡u\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡u-2\operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot v\operatorname{cos}⁡u \\  & =-2v({sin}^{2}⁡u+{cos}^{2}⁡u) \\  & =-2v.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14043620/assets/72902f1a278bc1316ff58c54940b4d5e65fa04aa8e1711c8e0a1726f57cd3641.png) the value of our Jacobian determinant is

$$
\left.\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}\right|_{(0,-1)} = -2(-1) = 2.
$$

feedback.problem: Find the Jacobian determinant of the transformation $T([\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}])=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{u+v} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(uv)\end{aligned}].$
feedback.worked_solution:
Given a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $x(u,v)={e}^{u+v}$ and $y(u,v)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(uv).$  

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={e}^{u+v} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & ={e}^{u+v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\frac{1}{u} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =\frac{1}{v}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{u+v} & {e}^{u+v} \\ \frac{1}{u} & \frac{1}{v}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{u+v}\cdot (\frac{1}{v})-{e}^{u+v}\cdot (\frac{1}{u}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{u+v}}{v}-\frac{{e}^{u+v}}{u} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{u+v}(u-v)}{vu}.\end{aligned}
$$
